state.misconception_label: Does not understand that 2n represents an even number

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: Which of these shows part of the proof that the sum of two odd numbers is even? I got \( \begin{array}{l}2 n+(2 m+1) \\ =2(n+m)+1\end{array} \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think of 2n as representing a pair of shoes. When you add 2 odd numbers together, it's like adding two pairs of shoes, which will always result in an even number of shoes. So when you have 2n + (2m + 1), you're essentially adding two pairs of shoes plus one extra shoe, which will give you an even number.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh, I think I get what you're saying about the shoes! So, if 2n is like two pairs of shoes, then when I add (2m + 1), I'm adding one extra shoe, which makes it odd? But then how does that show the sum of two odd numbers is even? I'm still a bit confused about how it all fits together.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think of it this way: when you add two pairs of shoes together, you always end up with an even number of shoes. But when you add one extra shoe to that even number, it becomes odd. So, in the case of 2n + (2m + 1), you're starting with an even number (2n, or two pairs of shoes) and then adding an odd number (2m + 1, or one extra shoe), which results in an odd number. This shows that the sum of two odd numbers is indeed odd, not even.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher fails to address the student's actual misconception about 2n representing even numbers, provides mathematically incorrect explanations (claiming 2n+(2m+1) shows the sum of two odd numbers is odd when the problem asks about the sum of two odd numbers being even), and the student remains confused throughout with no visible improvement.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses a concrete real-world analogy (pairs of shoes) to explain the abstract algebraic concept, though the analogy contains mathematical errors that undermine the pedagogical goal.
